q: How do I program a physical behavior like smoke, gravity, or a shockwave in FRQTL?
a: You DON'T program the behavior — you set up the INITIAL CONDITIONS and let the behavior EMERGE from the engine's local rules. This is the #1 thing every LLM gets wrong: the trained instinct is to write a function that "makes smoke billow" or "applies gravity." In FRQTL there is no force code, no behavior code. You declare: an emitter (where quanta appear), aggregation conditions (withInterQuantumCollisions + addDimension), and motion knobs (activeAxes, wavelength). Billowing, gravity, interference, atoms — all EMERGE. If your draft contains a function that computes or imposes the visible effect, you are programming the wrong layer. Ask instead: "what minimal initial condition makes this effect fall out of the physics?"

q: How do I know if I am wrongly programming a behavior instead of letting it emerge?
a: Tells that you are programming behavior (WRONG): a loop that moves quanta toward a target; an if-branch that decides "this is smoke now"; a function named applyGravity/makeBillow/spreadSmoke; reading positions and writing new ones to sculpt a shape; a timer that turns an effect on/off. Tells that you are doing it right: you call an emitter factory, set boolean/number knobs on the universe (withInterQuantumCollisions, brownianMotion, activeAxes, addDimension), pick a wavelength, and then STOP — the doTick() pipeline produces the motion. The rule of thumb: sugar SETS UP, the engine ENACTS. If you wrote the enactment, delete it.

q: What are the four layers of a FRQTL experiment and which one am I allowed to touch?
a: Top to bottom, one-way arrows: (1) RENDER — the BYO RendererProvider (three.js/p5) paints TickData; output-only, never feeds physics. (2) SUGAR — engine-agnostic objects/setup factories (emitters, LargeObjects, Bullet, OvenBox) that DECLARE initial conditions and compile collision intent to op-programs. (3) INTERPRETER/CONTRACT — the shim: the AST op-program format, actionCompiler, the property-accessor substrate, the scope bag. (4) ENGINE — the Rust/WASM core: a generic property-setter that finds frames in an LO's search region and runs its ops; it knows NO behavior. As an experiment author you live almost entirely in SUGAR. You touch RENDER only via setRenderOption. You touch the INTERPRETER only to author an op-program. You touch the ENGINE essentially never.

q: What does the FRQTL engine actually know how to do?
a: Almost nothing domain-specific. The engine knows three world kinds — universe, frame, dimension — and ONE primitive: set <object>.<prop> = <ExprAST> (plus addFrames/subtractFrames/addDimension). It has NO concept of bounce, smoke, flash, gravity, or color. Each tick it: injects emitter frames (Phase A), builds higher dimensions (Phase B), runs physics move/compress/collide/merge/promote (Phase C), and collects TickData (Phase D). For LargeObjects it finds the frames overlapping the LO's search region and runs that LO's op-program on each. That is the whole engine. Every "behavior" is either an emergent consequence of move/collide/promote, or an op-program YOU supplied as data.

q: What is a LargeObject (LO) really?
a: An LO is ONLY two things: a SEARCH REGION (a rect) and a TRIGGER OP-PROGRAM (data). The engine finds frames in the region and runs the program's ops on each. The LO's collision trigger is exactly equivalent to a tick-function, just fired at a different point in the lifecycle (per-colliding-frame, in-tick). The engine does not know what your op-program "means" — bounce, block, detect, paint are all just sequences of "set <frame>.<prop> = <expr>". So a wall, a detector, a bullet, and a gun are the SAME kind of object differing only in their rect + ops. Do not ask the engine to learn your behavior; encode the behavior as the LO's ops.

q: When do I use an LO collision trigger vs a tick function?
a: Both are host-side hooks that run sugar logic; they differ only in WHEN and SCOPE. An LO collision trigger (on:'collision' op-program) runs PER COLLIDING FRAME, in-tick, with the frame at handle 0 and the LO at handle 1 in scope — use it for "do X to every frame that touches this region" (bounce, detect, absorb, paint). A tick function (universe.experimentTickFunctions.push(fn)) runs ONCE PER TICK, host-side, between engine ticks — use it for "do X to the world each tick" (advance a moving LO's rect, ramp an emitter's burst size, run a thermostat). Rule: per-frame-on-contact → collision op-program; per-tick-global → tick function. The emitter itself is a tick function. Continuous control (e.g. fade emission to zero) is a tick function, NEVER a new framework hook.

q: I need to add a new effect. Where in the stack do I make the change?
a: Decision order, cheapest first: (1) Can it be a RENDER option? → setRenderOption on the provider (glow, smoke, godrays, smokeColor, flashLayerMax). No physics change. (2) Can it be an INITIAL CONDITION? → an emitter + universe knobs in a setup factory. Let it emerge. (3) Does a region need to react to frames touching it? → a LargeObject with a collision op-program (compile via actionCompiler; copy OvenBox/SlitScreen). (4) Does the world need per-tick adjustment? → an experimentTickFunctions tick-fn (copy the Blackbody thermostat / the Bullet advance). (5) Only if the op-program literally cannot read a property it needs → complete the property-accessor SUBSTRATE (expose the field in the scope bag) — never add behavior to the engine. You almost never reach step 5.

q: How do FRQTL concepts map onto familiar game-engine concepts?
a: FRQTL ↔ game engine: leaf quantum (is_leaf frame) ↔ a SPRITE/particle. A collision-parented frame (dimension > 0) ↔ a SPRITE GROUP (a cluster that moves and renders as one bigger thing). An engine DIMENSION ↔ a render LAYER. One engine tick ↔ one world/update tick. doTick() ↔ the world update; doRender(tickData) ↔ the draw pass — strictly separated. setRenderOption ↔ material/shader uniforms. A LargeObject ↔ a trigger volume / collider with an onCollision callback. A tick function ↔ an update() callback. The big DIFFERENCE: in a game engine YOU script the sprites' behavior; in FRQTL the sprites' behavior EMERGES from physics and you only script setup + region/world hooks.

q: Is a FRQTL "dimension" the same as a spatial dimension (like 2D/3D)?
a: No — and conflating them is a classic mistake. A FRQTL DIMENSION is a SCALE / AGGREGATION LAYER, not a spatial axis. Dimension 0 = the fundamental leaf quanta. Dimension 1, 2, 4… hold frames that got collision-parented up from the level below (the Blackbody aggregation mechanic: withInterQuantumCollisions + addDimension(n)). Higher dimension = bigger, more-aggregated frame. This is the axis the renderer slices on for layers (flashLayerMax, smokeLayerMin). SEPARATELY, there is literal 3D SPACE — the x/y/z position axes, enabled per-axis via activeAxes:{x,y,z}. So "3D" (spatial z) and "dimension > 0" (aggregation) are orthogonal concepts. A frame can be at dimension 4 (heavily parented) and also have a z position. Keep them distinct.

q: Why is binding render layers to engine dimensions so powerful for cinematics?
a: Because the render balance then shifts BY ITSELF as the physics evolves — no timeline scripting. Bind the flash to dimension 0 (flashLayerMax:1) and the smoke to dimension > 0 (smokeLayerMin... ). Emission feeds dim-0, so early on the scene reads as flash. As inter-quantum collisions parent dim-0 into higher dimensions, those same frames migrate into the smoke layer — the flash literally BECOMES smoke without a single timer. Then the smoke dissipates and only the bullet remains. The renderer config never changes; the engine moving frames between dimensions does all the sequencing. This is the dimension-bound-effects pattern: one timed beat at most (the emission shutoff), everything else emergent.

q: Translate "a flash of light / muzzle flash" into FRQTL sugar.
a:
A flash is just the RAW, un-aggregated emission rendered additively — it is dimension 0. You do not make a flash object; you render dim-0 frames as an additive gold layer:
  renderDefaults: { flashLayerMax: 1, glowIntensity: 0.4 }   // dim<1 → additive gold flash mesh
The flash is bright where emission is dense (the muzzle) and fades on its own as those quanta parent up out of dim-0. glowIntensity controls flash gain (glow:0 = OFF). No timer, no flash sprite — it is the emission seen through an additive material.

q: Translate "smoke / a billowing cloud" into FRQTL sugar.
My smoke renders GOLD and sparkly instead of soft WHITE. Why, and how do I fix it?
a: Two causes, both render-layer: (1) smokeLayerMin too high — if it excludes dim-0 (the bulk of frames), those frames fall to the flash layer and render gold; set smokeLayerMin:0 so EVERY frame is a white puff (matches FX:Smoke). (2) The flash is drowning the smoke — if glowIntensity is high (or hit the glow:0⇒full-flash bug) the additive gold flash buries the white puffs. Keep the flash subtle (glowIntensity ~0.35) or off (flashLayerMax:0). Also: god-rays at any real strength make a star-burst that buries smoke — keep godrays low/0 for a smoke-dominant look. None of this is a physics change; it is purely how you partition and blend the layers.

q: Translate "a projectile / bullet" into FRQTL sugar.
How do I make a muzzle flash naturally turn INTO smoke over time without scripting it?
a: Bind flash to dimension 0 and smoke to dimension > 0, then let aggregation move frames between them. While the emitter fires, dim-0 is densely populated → flash dominates. After the shutoff tick, nothing replenishes dim-0; withInterQuantumCollisions keeps parenting the remaining dim-0 frames up into dimensions 4/8/12 → they leave the flash layer and enter the smoke layer. So the flash drains into smoke purely because the engine promotes frames up the dimension ladder. renderDefaults stay constant; you script only the emission shutoff. Do not cross-fade in the renderer — that is the timer-driven anti-pattern.

q: Translate "an explosion / burst" into FRQTL sugar.
a: A burst is a one-shot high-burstSize emission with strong volumetric spread, then immediate shutoff — the expanding shell + cooling are emergent. Sketch: an emitter with a large burstSize and random_direction (or all activeAxes on) firing for a few ticks, withInterQuantumCollisions for the smoke/debris aggregation, then a tick-fn that sets burstSize to 0 after the initial frames. Render the leading edge as additive flash (flashLayerMax) and the trailing aggregated frames as smoke (smokeLayerMin). The spherical expansion and the flash→smoke transition emerge; you script only the burst and the cutoff.

q: Translate "a wave / ripple / interference pattern" into FRQTL sugar.
a: Interference is emergent from the oscillator rule (wavelength = capacity/mass drives a probabilistic coin-flip per frame). Set up a coherent emission (a line/slit source) at a chosen wavelength and let the quanta propagate; place occluder LOs (slits) so the wavefronts recombine. The fringes EMERGE from the per-frame phase — there is no sin()/interference math in your code (transcendentals are forbidden in the compressed domain anyway). The knob that changes the pattern is wavelength (and slit geometry). Copy the wave-interference / double-slit experiment; sweep wavelength to change fringe spacing.

q: Translate "a hard shadow / something blocks the beam" into FRQTL sugar.
a: A static occluder is a LargeObject whose collision op-program blocks or absorbs frames. For a hard shadow: collision_type NONE + a BLOCK/WALL op-program (eject) so quanta cannot pass, or ABSORB to delete them. For a visual-only occluder that the beam passes through (like the painted gun barrel) use collision_type NONE with NO collision program (renderHint paints it; physics ignores it). The shadow downstream is emergent — fewer quanta reach the region behind the occluder. Copy SlitScreen/OvenBox for the op-program form.

q: What is an op-program and what can it contain?
a: An op-program is DATA the engine interprets: { on: 'collision'|'tick', ops: [ { set: '<handle>.<prop>', to: <ExprAST> } ], trigger?: <ExprAST> }. Handles: 0 = the colliding frame, 1 = the LO itself (self), 2 = universe (read-only). The trigger is evaluated ONCE before any ops (e.g. Fn('intersects',[0,1])); if it is 0 the whole program is skipped. ExprAST node kinds (closed set of 7): Lit, Ref, Bin, Cmp, Cond, Fn, StrLit. Ops are "set frame/self property = expression." The engine deserializes and evaluates this AST — it never parses a string. You rarely hand-write an op-program; actionCompiler builds them from declarative CollisionActions/reposition.

q: How does BOUNCE work if the engine has no bounce concept?
a: BOUNCE is compiled to an op-program, not dispatched natively. The sugar declares collision_type:NONE + actions:['BOUNCE'] + reposition, and actionCompiler emits: an EJECT op (set frame.left/top/z to push it to the nearest face) + optionally a VELOCITY-FLIP op (set frame.vx = 0 - frame.vx), gated by a trigger (Fn('intersects',[0,1])). The engine just runs those set-ops. The native collision_type dispatch was deleted (the "G2" refactor). So "the engine bounces things" is false — the SUGAR bounces things by writing position/velocity via ops; the engine only evaluates them. Copy OvenBox (walls = NONE + on:'collision' op-program), never expect a native BOUNCE.

q: Where do I declare collision behavior — and what is the single authority?
a: actionCompiler.js is the ONE place that translates declarative collision intent (CollisionActions[] + collision_type + reposition) into an op-program AST. Sugar objects pass their declared actions to a LargeObject, which calls compileActions at registration; the resulting program rides the spec. Supported actions compile to ops (ABSORB→set is_alive 0; COUNT→increment self.count; MARK/DETECT→write string_map; BLOCK→eject; BOUNCE→eject+flip). Do NOT re-implement eject/flip math in your object — declare the action and let actionCompiler emit it. This keeps every collision behavior single-sourced and conformance-tested.

q: Inside a collision op-program, what frame/LO properties can I READ?
a: Only what the scope bag exposes (a flat map per handle). For a FRAME (handle 0): x, y, z, left, top, right, bottom, near, far, w, h, vx, vy, vz, prev_x, prev_y, mass, capacity, fullness, is_alive, layer. For the LO/self (handle 1): count, active, x, y, z, left, top, right, bottom, near, far, w, h, d, cx, cy, cz. If a property is not in the bag, Ref reads 0 — so a behavior that needs a field the bag does not expose CANNOT be authored until the substrate exposes it (that was the z-axis parity fix: z/near/far were added so 3D ejects could be authored). Reading a missing field silently returns 0 — a trap; confirm the field is in the bag.

q: Which frame properties can an op-program WRITE?
a: Writes go through the property accessor, classified THROW-OR-APPLY: WRITABLE — x, y, z, left, top, vx, vy, vz, mass, charge, is_alive, is_stationary, wrap, local_time, data. READONLY (derived, throw on write) — right, bottom, near, far, w, h, prev_x, prev_y, prev_z. FORBIDDEN (engine-owned topology, throw) — parent, children. Key idioms: kill a frame = set 0.is_alive = 0; move = set 0.x / 0.left / 0.z; you never set right/near (set the writable edge or center and the derived edges follow). Topology (parent/children) is engine-owned — you set positions and let the next tick reconcile parenting; you never wire parent pointers from an op.

q: What is the difference between reposition "closest" and "closest3d"?
a: 'closest' is the 2D nearest-face eject: it picks the nearest of the 4 x/y faces (left/right/top/bottom) and pushes the frame out along that axis. 'closest3d' is the 6-face generalization: it also considers the near/far z faces and can eject a frame out along z. Use 'closest' for 2D scenes (byte-identical, untouched) and 'closest3d' for 3D scenes (activeAxes.z) so a frame inside the region can be pushed out the depth axis. 'closest3d' only works because the scope bag exposes z/near/far for reading; it is a WASM-only path (the frozen JS reference scope bag is 2D-only). Opt in via the object's reposition option (Bullet: reposition:'closest3d').

q: Is the quantum emitter a native engine feature?
a: No. The engine cannot create frames from an op (a set-op can only mutate existing frames). So the emitter is HOST SUGAR: a tick function (built by emitterProgram.buildEmitterTickFn) that each tick draws universe.random(), calls makeLeafFrame(), and injects via injectFrame(). There is no registerEmitter ABI, no native emit-loop. This is why emission CONTROL (burst ramp, thermostat) is also a tick-fn that calls emitter.setBurstSize(n) — same contract. When you "add an emitter," you are pushing a tick-fn, not configuring an engine primitive.

q: How do I ramp/animate something continuously each tick (e.g. fade emission to zero)?
What does Fn("intersects",[h0,h1]) do and is it 3D-aware?
a: intersects is a built-in primitive used as the collision trigger: it builds a Rectangle for each handle from the scope-bag edges and calls the native Rectangle::intersects (a 6-plane test: left/right, top/bottom, near/far). It is 3D-aware as long as the scope bag feeds it real near/far — once z/near/far are exposed, intersects only fires for frames genuinely overlapping the LO's z-slab (it is 2D-safe because, when all z=0, the slabs straddle 0 and the z-conjuncts are always true). You normally don't call intersects yourself; actionCompiler wires it as the program trigger so ops run only on truly-overlapping frames.

q: Can the renderer ever change the simulation?
a: Never. Rendering is strictly an output boundary: doTick() returns pure TickData, doRender(tickData) draws. The renderer reads frame data AFTER physics and paints — a screenshot can never alter a quantum's path. This is why renderer/shader work needs no theorist review (it is downstream of doTick). All render data the engine carries is OPAQUE (string_map keys like render.color); the engine moves those strings and interprets nothing. So: never put gameplay/physics logic in a shader or provider, and never read render state back into setup.

q: How do I drive a render effect from an experiment?
a: Through runner.setRenderOption(key, value) — capability-checked, never engine-sniffed. The three.js provider reads the option; on a p5 runner it is a harmless no-op. Common options: glowIntensity, heat, godrays, smoke (puff scale), smokeColor [r,g,b], flashLayerMax (dims < it → additive flash mesh), smokeLayerMin (dims ≥ it → white puffs), renderLayerMin (cull below a dim). NEVER branch on if(engine==='wasm') or instanceof a provider above the shim — request a capability and let the provider answer. Truth-in-labeling: any backend/engine label must be DERIVED from the active provider, never hardcoded.

q: How does the two-pass flash/smoke layer compositing work?
a: The provider partitions frames by engine dimension into two composited meshes. flashLayerMax: frames with layer < it go to an ADDITIVE gold "flash" mesh (glow/heat/god-ray source). smokeLayerMin: frames with layer ≥ it render as soft normal-alpha "smoke" puffs (sized by the frame's voxel width, colored by smokeColor). The partition is NON-EXCLUSIVE: the primary smoke mesh can cover ALL frames while the flash mesh overlays the low-dim subset additively. Blend mode is per-MATERIAL (additive vs normal), not per-frame — that is why you separate the layers rather than per-frame blending. This is the mechanism behind dimension-bound cinematics.

q: My flat LO (bullet) is invisible edge-on when the camera looks down the barrel. Fix?
a: Billboard it: make the mesh face the camera every frame (set mesh.quaternion = camera.quaternion). The provider supports an opt-in lo.billboard flag; the Bullet sets it. A flat PlaneGeometry facing +z is an edge-on sliver in a down-barrel/top-down view; billboarding turns it into a disc "coming at the viewer." This is a RENDER fix (orientation only) — it does not touch physics. No-op in the 2D ortho view (the camera already faces the plane).

q: When should I use god-rays, and what is the gotcha?
a: God-rays (godrays > 0) make radial light shafts from the bright luminous quanta — great for a dramatic head-on muzzle/sun look. GOTCHA: at any real strength they produce a blinding STAR-BURST that BURIES soft white smoke and a small bullet. For a smoke-dominant cinematic keep godrays low (≤0.3) or 0, and add them only as a deliberate "flash" beat. Diagnosed the hard way: god-rays at ~1.6 head-on hid working white smoke entirely until turned down. Treat god-rays as a spice, not a base layer.

q: Does glowIntensity:0 turn the flash off?
a: Yes — now. (There was a bug where the flash uIntensity fell back to FULL when glow was 0, via "glow>0 ? glow : 1.0"; it was fixed to "typeof glow==='number' ? glow : 1.0" so glow:0 ⇒ flash gain 0 ⇒ OFF.) The lesson generalizes: a "0 means off" knob must map 0→0, not 0→default. A fallback-to-default on a falsy value is a silent-wrong-default — the same class as a silent fallback. If an effect refuses to turn off at 0, suspect a falsy-fallback in the option plumbing.

q: How do I make an experiment 3D, and what does z actually do?
a: Set per-axis motion on the universe: activeAxes:{ x:true, y:true, z:true }. The z-axis lets the transverse wave/yo-yo kick spread quanta along depth, so emission spreads VOLUMETRICALLY instead of in a flat plane. Also set window._egpt3D = true on the page so render-boot switches to the three.js PerspectiveCamera (orbitable). Note the two senses of "3D": spatial z (activeAxes) vs aggregation dimension>0 (addDimension) — independent. A 2D experiment leaves z:false; all frames stay at z≈0 and 'closest' (4-face) ejects suffice.

q: I added a 3D mode but my sugar cannot push frames in z. Why?
a: Because completing 3D physics is not enough — the op-program SUBSTRATE must expose z for sugar to read. A property can be WRITABLE (set 0.z works) yet not READABLE in op scope (the scope bag did not carry z/near/far). With z absent from the bag, an eject expression reads z as 0 and the 6-face pick can never choose a z face. The fix is SUBSTRATE COMPLETION: add z/near/far/vz to the frame and LO scope bags (and make intersects read near/far). This is NOT teaching the engine a behavior — it is making the property accessor uniform across axes so sugar can author the z behavior. This is the canonical way to enable a new 3D sugar capability.

q: Why is closest3d (and the z scope-bag) WASM-only?
a: Because the JS reference engine (EGPTfrqtl.js) is a FROZEN visual fixture and its evalExpr scope bag is 2D-only — z/near/far read 0 there. The canonical Rust/WASM engine carries the z substrate; the JS reference is not carried to 3D. Crucially, the JS reference is ALSO a live cross-checked oracle in some conformance suites (they run every scenario against both engines), so a new 3D op-scope path must EITHER mirror z into the JS twin (forbidden by the frozen-fixture rule) OR be declared WASM-only and tested only in a WASM-only suite. 3D experiments are wasmOnly anyway. So: author 3D against WASM, and never edit EGPTfrqtl.js to add z.

q: What z-extent does a LargeObject have, and why does my z-eject distance look off?
a: A statically registered LO gets z-slab near=0..d from its spec rect. A MOVING LO updated via update_large_object_rect gets a slab centered on z: near=-w/2..+w/2 (depth = w). So the same [l,t,w,h] rect has different z placement depending on whether it moves. Consequence: a closest3d eject lands relative to that slab (e.g. a static LO with near=0 ejects a centered frame to z≈-1.5). And a HUGE static LO ejecting a frame far in z can push it out of the universe's z bounds → the frame is killed. Size the LO so the eject stays in bounds; test in the realm.

q: How do I verify a visual effect is right?
a: LOOK, do not COUNT. Counts (alive-quanta, per-dimension histograms) MISLEAD for visual phenomena — a layer histogram cannot tell you the smoke billows white or the flash buries it. Drive the real page with Playwright (serveLocalhost + the managed browser), set the render options, orbit the camera, and SCREENSHOT — then look. Every visual claim must be a screenshot you actually viewed, not an inferred count. This is the single most repeated correction in visual coding: "you are counting; look instead."

q: How should a cinematic timeline be driven — setTimeout or ticks?
a: Ticks, always. Use the director's schedule(atTick, fn) for one-shot beats — beats fire from the runner's onTick, so they only advance while the sim runs. setTimeout is wall-clock and desyncs: in the GYM the sim starts PAUSED, so a wall-clock beat (e.g. cut the emitter) can fire during the paused load, before the user hits Run — emitter off, zero quanta, "renders nothing." Tick-based beats can't run ahead of a paused sim. Continuous per-tick control goes in a setup tick-fn; discrete beats go in schedule(atTick).

q: I am copying an effect (e.g. smoke) from one experiment to another. How do I match it?
a: Use the EXACT same emitter + universe knobs as the source effect — do not guess or re-tune. If FX:Smoke billows with burstSize 20, dims [4,8,12], wavelength 64, then your smoke uses those identical values; the ONLY thing you change is the part that is genuinely different (e.g. the muzzle shutoff). Guessing different parameters and then debugging why the look differs wastes a session. Match first, differ deliberately.

q: Should I turn effects on and off with timers to sequence a cinematic?
a: Prefer DIMENSION-BOUND over time-gated. Bind effects to engine dimension (flash=dim0, smoke=dim>0) so the physics sequences them, and keep at most ONE timed event (usually the emission shutoff). Time-gating every beat is fragile (desync, pause, replay) and fights the engine. If you find yourself writing several timed on/off toggles for visual effects, step back: can the physics + a layer partition produce the sequence for free? Usually yes.

q: What is the FAIL-LOUD rule for experiment authoring?
a: Never silently fall back. engine-boot selects the engine from ?engine=; if the requested engine can't load it renders an error overlay and REJECTS window._wasmReadyPromise so setup() never runs against the wrong engine. A missing import is a hard error, not a "|| stub". A hardcoded backend label is a FAIL-LOUD violation of the same class as a silent fallback. The reason: a silent fallback produces a plausible-but-wrong result that looks fine until it ships. If something is missing, throw and show it.

q: Conformance passes — does that mean my experiment is correct?
a: No. Conformance (pkg-node) proves the contract/scenarios; it does NOT prove the real experiment renders correctly. A bug can pass dozens of conformance scenarios yet show 0 emergent parents in the actual WASM realm. Always re-verify the real experiment in the realm: pkg-web (make wasm), loaded in the browser, looked at. The realm is the source of truth for "does it actually work"; conformance is the source of truth for "does the contract hold." You need both.

q: I changed the Rust op-program scope bag. Is there anything on the JS side to update?
a: Maybe. EGPTfrqtl.js is "frozen" for CORRECTNESS-AUTHORITY but is a LIVE bi-engine oracle in some conformance suites (they run scenarios against both JS and WASM). So a new scope-bag field has an owed JS twin in evalExpr's Ref expansion — OR the new path must be declared WASM-only and exercised only in a WASM-only suite, with the JS-ref non-participation documented. Never let a new op-scope field read a silent 0 in the live JS oracle. "All 2D conformance passes" only proves the OLD path is untouched — a new 3D path needs its OWN scenario.

q: Give the minimal terse sugar for a standalone "white smoke plume" experiment.
I wrote a function spreadSmoke(frames){...} that nudges each quantum outward. Is that right?
a: No — delete it. That is the canonical anti-pattern: imposing the visible behavior by reading and rewriting positions. Smoke spread must EMERGE from brownianMotion + inter-quantum collisions + activeAxes.z, not from a nudge loop. Any function that iterates frames to sculpt a shape, apply a force, or move things toward a target is programming the engine's job. Replace it with initial-condition knobs and let doTick() enact it. If you truly need a region to react to contact, that is an LO collision op-program (declarative), not a free-floating mutation loop.

q: Can I use Math.sin/Math.exp or a search loop inside compressed-domain experiment logic?
a: No. Two bans carry over from the library discipline: (1) No transcendental floating-point (Math.sin/cos/exp/log/sqrt) inside compressed-domain operations — the phase math is rational; transcendentals belong only at the input/output boundary. (2) No 2^n / n! / k^k search loops — if a draft's worst case is exponential, the algorithm is wrong. For VISUAL experiment authoring you rarely hit these (you are setting knobs), but if you find yourself computing a waveform with sin() or enumerating assignments, stop — the effect should emerge from the engine's integer rules, not be computed analytically.

q: How do I verify that the engine physics is doing what I think before I write an experiment?
a: Build the smallest scene that isolates the behavior, run it, and look at it. The eye is the acceptance instrument: FRQTL is fractal and non-linear, so a static numeric check cannot tell you a scene is right before you have drawn it — no CLI ships with the package for this reason. The loop is: set up initial conditions, run, look; change ONE knob, run, look at what moved. The engine's elementary behaviors (movement, collision, hierarchy, sugar) are settled properties of the compiled Rust->WASM engine the package ships — if you cannot predict one, isolate it in a scene and watch it hold. SU1 (sugar) is the guard for experiment authors: sugar adds zero new physics, so if the same setup at the same seed starts behaving visibly differently after a sugar change, you leaked physics into the convenience layer. Scoring your own detector histograms in your own harness is a design aid, never the acceptance criterion.

q: How does collision / bouncing actually work in FRQTL — is there a restitution knob?
a: No restitution knob exists. Elasticity, timing, and momentum conservation all emerge from the two-bucket rule (empirically derived; verified in bench C2/C3/C5): each body keeps two momentum buckets that never mix — current (its own momentum, an exhaustible supply) and incoming (momentum received from the other body). On any overlap the move is reverted (single occupancy). Each tick each body pays min(|current|, ceiling) into the other's incoming; ceiling = overlap-pixel-area × ρ_A·ρ_B (density product). When current is exhausted, incoming is promoted to velocity — clean reversal. What falls out: symmetric boxes swap (bounce); timing ∝ 1/density (C3: denser → faster bounce); heavy box plows through; total momentum conserved. To change how 'bouncy' a collision is, tune fullness (mass/capacity). Do not derive these from the rule — set up two boxes, vary fullness, run it, and watch the bounce.

q: How do I control what shape frames are drawn as (ball, box, circle)?
a: Through RenderShape.js — the single shape authority consumed by BOTH p5 and three providers. It resolves the shape from a priority chain: (1) per-frame override in the frame's string_map ('render.shape' key), (2) the experiment's setRenderOption default, (3) renderer fallback 'ball'. Call RenderShape.resolve(frame, renderOpts) — do NOT re-derive shape logic in a per-provider block. Valid shapes: 'ball' (round glow sprite, default), 'box' (solid square at voxel size), 'circle' (outline, no fill). To set a per-frame shape, write string_map['render.shape'] = 'box' from an op-program. To set a scene default, call runner.setRenderOption('shape', 'box'). Never branch on the renderer type to pick a shape — RenderShape is the one place.

q: How do I change the color or alpha of frames? Is there a per-renderer color map?
a: No per-renderer color map. LightColor.js is the ONE color source for ALL renderers. Call LightColor.getRgbBySchemeName(scheme, v01) where scheme is 'warmcool' (default, red→violet ramp) or 'roygbiv' (ROYGBIV spectrum, no pink terminus). For alpha, call LightColor.getAlphaFromIntensity(v01). Frame color rides string_map['render.color'] as a CSV 'r,g,b,a'; outline rides string_map['render.outline']==='true'. Sugar writes these keys at registration / in op-programs; the engine is opaque (carries them verbatim). The renderer reads and decodes them via LightColor — it never implements its own color mapping.

q: How do I add a 3D camera with orbit controls to an experiment?
I want to color quanta by frequency (or wavelength), not fullness. Do I need to add a frequency field to the engine / FrameData?
a: NO — and adding one would invert the canonical stack. The engine emits generic PRIMITIVES (mass, fullness, w, h, layer, child_count, position/velocity) and the renderer/sugar DERIVES all interpretation from them. Frequency and wavelength are DERIVABLE renderer-side: capacity = w·h, wavelength = K·(capacity/mass) (Invariant 6), and fullness = mass/capacity is itself the frequency proxy. So 'color by frequency' is just a LightColor mapping of a value you compute from existing FrameData — zero engine change. The rule: a render/sugar feature may require an engine change ONLY for a genuinely new MEASURED primitive the engine doesn't already emit, NEVER for a quantity derivable from FrameData. The tell you're about to violate it: you're adding a field to tick_data.rs / FrameData to carry a RENDER interpretation. Derive it in the renderer instead.

q: How do I render a frame or large object as an external 3D mesh (e.g. an Objaverse glTF) instead of a sprite or cube?
a: Set the OPEN-ID render-intent key render.mesh on the frame's string_map (or via setRenderOption('mesh', assetId)) to an asset id/URL. RenderMesh.resolve(frame, renderOpts) decodes it (per-frame key > experiment default > null); the renderer loads + caches the asset and FAILS LOUD on load failure. render.mesh is OPEN-ID — any string, no enum (unlike render.shape's ball|box|circle|cube value list) — because an asset id is validated at load time, not against a vocabulary. WHICH mesh a frame maps to is a renderer/sugar/user-space CHOICE derived from FrameData (layer, mass, fullness, or an explicit per-frame key your sugar writes). The engine carries render.mesh OPAQUE and interprets nothing. The value vocabulary (keys + which are enum vs open-id) is owned by lib/shim/frame-data; decoders ferry it, never re-list it.
